lec05kp18-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp18-u01-p1-title.text: A Parzen estimate averages kernels: one neuron per training point

lec05kp18-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p1-bridge.text: The networks of KP17 all need training. Is there a network that needs almost no training?

lec05kp18-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-parzen
lec05kp18-u01-p1-fig1.text: Five one-dimensional training points each carry a Gaussian kernel (thin lines) whose average is the estimated density (thick line), width 0.4.

image.alt: Five one-dimensional training points each carry a Gaussian kernel (thin lines) whose average is the estimated density (thick line), width 0.4.

lec05kp18-u01-p1-term:Parzen 估計.name: term:Parzen estimate
lec05kp18-u01-p1-term:Parzen 估計.text: **Parzen estimate**: a kernel (Gaussian here) on every training point, averaged to estimate the class density $\hat p(x\mid\omega)$.

lec05kp18-u01-p1-term:核寬.name: term:Kernel width
lec05kp18-u01-p1-term:核寬.text: **Kernel width $h$**: the width of the kernel; larger is smoother and smaller hugs the individual training points.

lec05kp18-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p1-c2.text: **The idea**: a sum of kernels is easy to compute in parallel, so why not one neuron per training point in a network?

lec05kp18-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp18-u01-p2-title.text: Normalize to length 1 and the squared distance collapses to an inner product, ‖x − xᵢ‖² = 2 − 2xᵢᵀx

lec05kp18-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p2-bridge.text: Every kernel of the Parzen estimate needs the distance from $x$ to a training point. Neurons are best at inner products, so can the distance become an inner product?

lec05kp18-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-circle
lec05kp18-u01-p2-fig1.text: Two vectors x=(0.6,0.8) and xᵢ=(1,0) on the unit circle with the chord between them: squared distance 0.8 = 2 − 2×0.6.

image.alt: Two vectors x=(0.6,0.8) and xᵢ=(1,0) on the unit circle with the chord between them: squared distance 0.8 = 2 − 2×0.6.

lec05kp18-u01-p2-term:單位範數正規化.name: term:Unit-norm normalization
lec05kp18-u01-p2-term:單位範數正規化.text: **Unit-norm normalization**: divide every feature vector by its own length $\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum_jx_j^2}$ so that its length becomes 1.

lec05kp18-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p2-c2.text: **Example**: $x=(0.6,0.8)$, $x_i=(1,0)$: inner product $0.6$ and squared distance $2-1.2=0.8$; directly $(0.4)^2+0.8^2=0.8$, the same.

lec05kp18-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp18-u01-p3-title.text: The Gaussian kernel becomes exp((xᵢᵀx − 1)/h²): the two forms agree only after normalization

lec05kp18-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p3-bridge.text: The distance became an inner product. What do the Gaussian kernel and the Bayes discriminant become, and is there a condition?

lec05kp18-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-kernels
lec05kp18-u01-p3-fig1.text: The Gaussian kernel in distance form and inner-product form: both 0.5353 for a unit vector and 0.1312 against 1.3668 for the non-unit vector (1.2,1.6).

image.alt: The Gaussian kernel in distance form and inner-product form: both 0.5353 for a unit vector and 0.1312 against 1.3668 for the non-unit vector (1.2,1.6).

lec05kp18-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p3-c2.text: **Check** ($h=0.8$): for the unit vector $x=(0.6,0.8)$ the distance form and the inner-product form both give $0.5353$.

lec05kp18-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp18-u01-p3-c3.text: **The condition**: for the non-unit $x=(1.2,1.6)$ the forms give $0.1312$ and $1.3668$, far apart; normalization is required.

lec05kp18-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp18-u01-p4-title.text: The architecture: one hidden node per training point, with the training vector itself as the weights

lec05kp18-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p4-bridge.text: The Gaussian kernel now has an inner product form. The discriminant is an inner product, an activation and a weighted sum: which layer of a network does each part correspond to?

lec05kp18-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-arch
lec05kp18-u01-p4-fig1.text: PNN architecture: two input nodes, five hidden nodes (three of class A and two of class B) and two output nodes, each output connected only to the hidden nodes of its class.

image.alt: PNN architecture: two input nodes, five hidden nodes (three of class A and two of class B) and two output nodes, each output connected only to the hidden nodes of its class.

lec05kp18-u01-p4-term:機率神經網路.name: term:Probabilistic neural network
lec05kp18-u01-p4-term:機率神經網路.text: **Probabilistic neural network** (PNN): the formula above moved into a network, one hidden node per training point and one output node per class, with weights taken directly from the training data.

lec05kp18-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p4-c1.text: **Hidden layer**: $N$ nodes, the weights of node $k$ are the $k$-th training vector and its output is $y_k=\exp\!\big((x_k^Tx-1)/h^2\big)$ (the $\exp$ is the activation).

lec05kp18-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p4-c2.text: **Output layer**: one linear combiner per class connected only to the hidden nodes of that class: $\text{out}_m=\tfrac{P(\omega_m)}{N_m}\sum y_k$; the largest wins.

lec05kp18-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp18-u01-p5-title.text: A full worked example: five training vectors, a test vector at 70°, class A's 0.294 beats class B's 0.206

lec05kp18-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p5-bridge.text: The architecture has one hidden node per training point. Work through five training vectors: which class has the larger output?

lec05kp18-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-toy
lec05kp18-u01-p5-fig1.text: The toy example with a test vector at 70°: five hidden outputs and an A output of 0.2943 larger than the B output of 0.2062.

image.alt: The toy example with a test vector at 70°: five hidden outputs and an A output of 0.2943 larger than the B output of 0.2062.

lec05kp18-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p5-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): class A at $20°,40°,60°$, class B at $100°,120°$, test vector at $70°$, $h=0.5$, priors 0.5; all lengths are 1 and A has 3 points against 2, hence the division by $N_m$.

lec05kp18-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp18-u01-p6-title.text: The kernel width: only a very small h hurts, about 91.6% on new points for h from 0.1 to 1

lec05kp18-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p6-bridge.text: In the worked example with five training vectors $h=0.5$ classified correctly. What value of $h$ is good, and what happens if it is larger or smaller?

lec05kp18-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-hcurve
lec05kp18-u01-p6-fig1.text: PNN accuracy against kernel width h on training and new points: 89.6% on new points at h=0.02 and about 91.6% for h from 0.1 to 1, with the dashed line at 91.9% for a single cut at 75°.

image.alt: PNN accuracy against kernel width h on training and new points: 89.6% on new points at h=0.02 and about 91.6% for h from 0.1 to 1, with the dashed line at 91.9% for a single cut at 75°.

lec05kp18-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p6-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): two classes distinguished by direction (means $40°$ and $110°$, sd $25°$) with random lengths; 50 training and 500 new points per class, normalized and fed to a PNN.

lec05kp18-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p6-c2.text: **Result**: $h=0.02$ gives 95% on training (the classes overlap, so never 100%) and 89.6% on new points (hugging single points); $h=0.1\sim1$ gives about 91.6%; $h=5$ still gives 91.0%.

lec05kp18-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp18-u01-p6-c3.text: **Reference**: a single cut at $75°$ gets 91.9% on new points and the PNN is close to it; this easy example is insensitive to $h$.

lec05kp18-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp18-u01-p7-title.text: 10 points per class reach 91.8%, more hardly helps

lec05kp18-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p7-bridge.text: Only a very small $h$ hurts, so the kernel width is not critical. With one hidden node per training point, how many points must be kept?

lec05kp18-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-nsub
lec05kp18-u01-p7-fig1.text: Accuracy on new points for 2, 5, 10, 25, 50 and 200 training points per class (mean and sd of 20 draws): from 88.3% to 92.0%.

image.alt: Accuracy on new points for 2, 5, 10, 25, 50 and 200 training points per class (mean and sd of 20 draws): from 88.3% to 92.0%.

lec05kp18-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p7-c1.text: **Experiment** (designed here): the same data with $n$ training points per class, $h=0.3$, 20 random draws each.

lec05kp18-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp18-u01-p7-c3.text: **Meaning**: this easy data need not be kept in full; fewer points mean a smaller network. The numbers differ slightly from the last page because the training data were redrawn.

lec05kp18-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp18-u01-p8-title.text: The price: the hidden layer is as large as the training set, N×l multiply-adds per prediction

lec05kp18-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p8-bridge.text: Ten points per class were enough. But a PNN usually keeps every training point, so what does it cost?

lec05kp18-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-cost
lec05kp18-u01-p8-fig1.text: Cost table: N=100, l=2 takes 200 operations and 1.6 KB; N=10⁴, l=10 takes 10⁵ and 0.8 MB; N=10⁶, l=100 takes 10⁸ and 0.8 GB.

image.alt: Cost table: N=100, l=2 takes 200 operations and 1.6 KB; N=10⁴, l=10 takes 10⁵ and 0.8 MB; N=10⁶, l=100 takes 10⁸ and 0.8 GB.

lec05kp18-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p8-c1.text: **Work and memory**: each test point needs $N\cdot l$ multiply-adds and $N\cdot l$ stored numbers (8 bytes each).

lec05kp18-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p8-c2.text: **Examples**: $N=100,l=2$: 200 operations, 1.6 KB; $N=10^4,l=10$: $10^5$ operations, 0.8 MB; $N=10^6,l=100$: $10^8$ operations, 0.8 GB.

lec05kp18-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp18-u01-p8-c3.text: **To remember**: PNN = a parallel hardware version of the Parzen estimate; training is copying data and inference computes everything. It sits at one end of a spectrum with sparsification (KP21): keep all against keep only the support vectors.

lec05kp18-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp18-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: normalization discards the length, and a PNN gets only 49.5% when the classes differ only in length

lec05kp18-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p9-bridge.text: Keeping everything costs $N\times l$ multiply-adds per prediction. A PNN also needs the vectors normalized to length 1; what if the length carries the class information?

lec05kp18-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-rings
lec05kp18-u01-p9-fig1.text: Left: two concentric rings that differ only in radius; right: after normalization both classes sit on the unit circle and the PNN is only 49.5% right.

image.alt: Left: two concentric rings that differ only in radius; right: after normalization both classes sit on the unit circle and the PNN is only 49.5% right.

lec05kp18-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp18-u01-p9-c1.text: **Example** (designed here): concentric rings whose classes differ only in radius (about 1.0 against 2.2), 200 points each, half for training and half for testing.

lec05kp18-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp18-u01-p9-c2.text: **Result**: after normalization both classes sit on the unit circle with the same angle distribution and the PNN gets only 49.5% on new points, which is guessing.

lec05kp18-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp18-u01-p9-c3.text: **So**: normalization discards the length; before using a PNN check that the class information lies in the direction and not in the length.

lec05kp18-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp18-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, two training vectors and the kernel width

lec05kp18-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p10-bridge.text: A PNN fails when the length carries the class information. Back to the case where the direction carries it, with two training vectors: which class does it give for $h=1$ and for $h=0.2$?

lec05kp18-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-practice
lec05kp18-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: training vectors (1,0) and (0,1), test vector (0.8,0.6); which class for h=1 and h=0.2.

image.alt: Practice figure: training vectors (1,0) and (0,1), test vector (0.8,0.6); which class for h=1 and h=0.2.

lec05kp18-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp18-u01-p10-q1.text: **Setup**: training vectors $x_A=(1,0)$ and $x_B=(0,1)$, test vector $x=(0.8,0.6)$, priors 0.5; $y_k=\exp((x_k^Tx-1)/h^2)$.

lec05kp18-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp18-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: for $h=0.2$, which class, and how does the ratio of the outputs change?

lec05kp18-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp18-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp18-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp18-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked which class two training vectors give for $h=1$ and $h=0.2$. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp18-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp18-practice-sol
lec05kp18-u01-p11-fig1.text: h=1: outputs 0.409 against 0.335, class A; h=0.2: 0.0034 against 0.00002, class A with a ratio of about 148.

image.alt: h=1: outputs 0.409 against 0.335, class A; h=0.2: 0.0034 against 0.00002, class A with a ratio of about 148.

lec05kp18-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp18-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2** ($h=0.2$): $y_A=e^{-5}=0.0067$ and $y_B=e^{-10}=0.000045$; outputs $0.0034$ against $0.00002$, still class A, with the ratio growing from 1.22 to about 148.

lec05kp18-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp18-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the smaller the $h$ the more a near training point is magnified and a far one suppressed; the ratio at $h=1$ is $0.819/0.670=1.22$.

steps.label: PNN
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The discriminant, the unit-norm simplification, the architecture, the cost and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (the checks 0.5353 and 0.1312/1.3668, the 70-degree toy, the kernel-width and training-size experiments, the cost table, the failure on rings) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added), and the page states honestly the easy example that is insensitive to the kernel width and the limit that normalization discards the length. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: One neuron per point
steps.speakerNotes: KP17 compared who can approximate a function, and those networks all need training. This page asks whether there is a network that needs almost no training. Two terms first: a Parzen estimate puts a kernel on every training point, Gaussian here, and averages them to estimate the class density; the kernel width h is the width of the kernel, larger is smoother and smaller hugs the individual training points. The Bayes decision compares the largest prior times Parzen estimate. The idea: the sum of kernels can be computed in parallel anyway, so why not one neuron per training point and let a network do it? The figure shows five training points each with a Gaussian kernel whose average is the estimated density. The next page asks whether the distance in each kernel can become the inner product that neurons do best.

steps.label: Distance becomes inner product
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said every kernel needs the distance. This page asks whether the distance can become an inner product, the thing neurons do best. First unit-norm normalization: divide every feature vector by its own length so that the length becomes 1. Expand the squared distance: the squared length of x plus the squared length of x_i minus 2 times the inner product; with both lengths 1 it equals 2 minus 2 times the inner product. Example: x equal to (0.6, 0.8) and x_i equal to (1, 0): the inner product is 0.6 and the squared distance is 2 minus 1.2, which is 0.8; directly 0.4 squared plus 0.8 squared is also 0.8, the same. The figure shows two vectors on the unit circle and the chord between them. The next page asks what the Gaussian kernel and the discriminant become.

steps.label: The discriminant
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the distance became an inner product. This page asks what the Gaussian kernel and the Bayes discriminant become and whether there is a condition. The discriminant: the prior over N_m times the sum of exponentials whose exponent is x_i transpose x minus 1 over h squared, with common constants dropped. Check with h equal to 0.8: for the unit vector x equal to (0.6, 0.8) the distance form and the inner-product form both give 0.5353. The condition: for x equal to (1.2, 1.6), not a unit vector, the distance form gives 0.1312 and the inner-product form gives 1.3668, far apart, so normalization is required. The next page asks which layer of a network this formula corresponds to.

steps.label: The architecture
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the discriminant is an inner product, an activation and a weighted sum. This page asks which layer of a network each part corresponds to. First the probabilistic neural network, PNN for short: the formula above moved into a network, one hidden node per training point and one output node per class, with weights taken directly from the training data. Hidden layer: N nodes, the weights of node k are the k-th training vector and the output y_k is e to the x_k transpose x minus 1 over h squared. Output layer: one linear combiner per class connected only to the hidden nodes of that class, the output being the prior over N_m times the sum of the y, and the largest wins. This network needs almost no training: no gradient descent, no local minima, no epochs. The next page works through five training vectors.

steps.label: A full worked example
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page put the architecture in place. This page asks which class has the larger output when five training vectors are worked through. The setup was designed here: class A at 20, 40 and 60 degrees, class B at 100 and 120 degrees, a test vector at 70 degrees, h equal to 0.5 and priors of 0.5. Hidden outputs: A gives 0.2396, 0.5851 and 0.9410; B gives 0.5851 and 0.2396. Outputs: A is 0.5 over 3 times 1.7658, which is 0.2943; B is 0.5 over 2 times 0.8247, which is 0.2062; A wins. The intuition is that 70 degrees is close to the 60 degrees of class A. The next page asks what value of the kernel width h is good.

steps.label: The kernel width
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said h equal to 0.5 classified correctly in the toy example. This page asks what value of h is good and what happens if it is larger or smaller. The setup was designed here: two classes distinguished by direction, means 40 and 110 degrees with standard deviation 25 degrees, random lengths, 50 training and 500 new points per class, normalized and fed to a PNN. Results: h equal to 0.02 gives 95% on training and 89.6% on new points, hugging single points; h from 0.1 to 1 gives about 91.6% on new points; h equal to 5 still gives 91.0%. Reference: a single cut at 75 degrees gets 91.9% on new points and the PNN is close to it. Honestly, this easy example is insensitive to h and only a very small h hurts. The next page asks how many training points to keep.

steps.label: How many points
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the result is insensitive to h. This page asks how many training points need to be kept when every point is a hidden node. The experiment was designed here: the same data with n training points per class, h equal to 0.3, 20 random draws each. Mean accuracy on new points: 88.3% with standard deviation 0.07 for n equal to 2, 91.8% with 0.011 for n equal to 10, 92.0% for n equal to 50 and 92.0% for n equal to 200. The meaning is that this easy data need not be kept in full; fewer points mean a smaller network. The next page asks the cost of keeping everything.

steps.label: The cost
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said ten points per class were enough. This page asks the cost since a PNN usually keeps every training point. Each test point needs N times l multiply-adds and N times l stored numbers of 8 bytes. Examples: N equal to 100 and l equal to 2 takes 200 operations and 1.6 KB; N equal to 10 thousand and l equal to 10 takes 10 to the 5 operations and 0.8 MB; N equal to 1 million and l equal to 100 takes 10 to the 8 operations and 0.8 GB. To remember: a PNN is a parallel hardware version of the Parzen estimate, training is copying data and inference computes everything, moving the learning cost to the inference cost; it lies at one end of a spectrum with sparsification, in KP21: keep all against keep only the support vectors. The next extension page looks at the price of normalization.

steps.label: Extension: normalization
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said keeping everything is a cost. This extension asks what happens when the length carries the class information, since a PNN also needs the vectors normalized to length 1. The example was designed here: concentric rings whose classes differ only in radius, about 1.0 against 2.2, 200 points each, half for training and half for testing. The result: after normalization both classes sit on the unit circle with the same angle distribution and the PNN gets only 49.5% on new points, which is guessing. So normalization discards the length, and before using a PNN you must check that the class information lies in the direction and not in the length. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a PNN fails when the length carries the class information. This page poses an exercise back in the case where the direction carries it: training vectors x_A equal to (1, 0) and x_B equal to (0, 1), a test vector x equal to (0.8, 0.6), priors of 0.5 and y_k equal to e to the x_k transpose x minus 1 over h squared. Question 1: for h equal to 1, which class? Question 2: for h equal to 0.2, which class, and how does the ratio of the outputs change? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1, h equal to 1: the inner product of x_A with x is 0.8 and that of x_B with x is 0.6; y_A is e to the minus 0.2, which is 0.819, and y_B is e to the minus 0.4, which is 0.670; the outputs 0.409 against 0.335 give class A. Question 2, h equal to 0.2: y_A is e to the minus 5, which is 0.0067, and y_B is e to the minus 10, which is 0.000045; the outputs 0.0034 against 0.00002 still give class A, with the ratio growing from 1.2 to about 148. Check: the smaller the h the more a near training point is magnified and a far one suppressed. That finishes the PNN; the next knowledge point looks at the nonlinear SVM and the Mercer kernel trick.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP18: the probabilistic neural network (PNN), moving the Parzen estimate into a network (undergraduate, self-study)
